analysis.title: Macro Comment Global: Mind the gap...
key_insights: Market pricing of policy rates is well above professional forecasts for the Fed, ECB, Bank of England and Riksbank. The gap is among the largest in 20 years.

For the Fed, markets price slightly more than three hikes from here against one expected by forecasters. That is about 50bp apart at end-2027 and more than 1 percentage point further out, since consensus has the Fed cutting again in 2028.
The gap is 60-125bp at the far end in all four economies, which points to a common global driver of the premium rather than country-specific growth or inflation views.

Handelsbanken says risk skew alone (market pricing is a probability-weighted average, forecasts are base cases) cannot explain a gap this large and persistent, so much of it is a premium for protection against higher rates.

Supply shocks turn the stock-bond correlation positive: energy prices rise, inflation expectations and rates rise, and bonds and equities fall together. Bonds then stop hedging equities and portfolio risk rises.
A positive stock-bond correlation was the norm from the mid-1960s to around 2000. A negative correlation has been the exception, and whether inflation risk or growth risk dominates decides its sign.

For a 60/40 portfolio, a 25bp rise in US 10-year yields costs about 0.8% on the bond leg. Pre-pandemic, equities tended to rise with yields and left the portfolio slightly up. Over the summer the same rise implied a loss above 2%, about three times the bond loss alone.

US Treasuries rose about 0.35% on average on days the S&P 500 fell more than 1% before the pandemic. In 2023-25 the gain was about a third of that. In 2022 bonds fell on such days, and from the March oil shock to September they fell almost 0.4% on average.

Since the October tech sell-off the hedge has returned, with bonds rising on six of seven bad days. The Fed premium shrank from well over 100bp to about 30bp. In November the stock-bond correlation has started to rise again.

Investors without a bond hedge buy rate protection in derivatives. Dealers on the other side demand compensation, which pushes market-implied rates above the expected path. The difference is the premium.

The Fed premium has tracked the stock-bond correlation since early 2025. It built after the March 2026 oil shock and at times exceeded 100bp. Handelsbanken estimates a move from negative to positive correlation corresponds to a premium about 40bp larger. It finds no evidence the premium is larger when central banks are hiking (data back to 2006).
Apart from the financial crisis, the Fed premium has not been this high since the 2006 sample start. The ECB premium has only been higher in 2022.
Market pricing is a less reliable guide than usual to where central banks will take rates, so forecasts deserve more weight.

The premium spreads to other short-term rates and to currencies through rate differentials. It currently looks larger in the UK and eurozone than in Sweden, which implies upside for the krona when the premium fades.

November market pricing rose after a surprisingly high US inflation print and hawkish comments from several Fed officials. The forecasts in the charts are from October, so week-to-week changes in the gap say little.

De-escalation in the Middle East and lower energy prices could shrink the premium quickly, so market-implied rates could fall by more than policy expectations alone. An escalation or a longer road to a deal would keep the regime in place and could widen the premium.
More frequent supply shocks since the pandemic mean the premium may return whenever one hits. It also tightens financial conditions, doing some of the central banks' work.

macro_indicators.indicator: Fed policy rate, market pricing vs consensus
macro_indicators.reading: Market prices slightly more than three hikes from here; consensus expects one hike
macro_indicators.interpretation: Gap of about 50bp at end-2027 and more than 1 percentage point further out, with consensus cutting in 2028. Handelsbanken attributes much of it to a premium for rate protection.
The similar size across four economies suggests a common global driver.

macro_indicators.indicator: Fed premium (market-implied rate one year ahead minus consensus)
macro_indicators.reading: At times above 100bp after the March 2026 oil shock; about 30bp after the October tech sell-off
macro_indicators.interpretation: Highest since 2006 apart from the financial crisis. It rose again in November.

macro_indicators.reading: Described as surprisingly high, no figure given
macro_indicators.interpretation: Pushed market pricing of policy rates up again in November along with hawkish Fed comments.

risk_factors: Escalation in the Middle East or a longer road to a deal keeps inflation risk in focus and the premium elevated or wider.
Recurring supply shocks since the pandemic could bring the premium back after any resolution.
Stocks and bonds falling together raises portfolio risk, and a 60/40 portfolio lost more than 2% on a 25bp rise in yields this summer.
Further hawkish Fed communication and high US inflation prints could push market pricing higher.
charts_described: Charts of Fed, ECB, Bank of England and Riksbank policy rates show market pricing above consensus based on the median of Bloomberg's October survey, with gaps above 100bp in some instances.
Chart of the Fed premium against the stock-bond correlation since 2025 shows the premium tracking the correlation, building after the March 2026 oil shock.
The 60/40 chart shows a 25bp rise in US 10-year yields leaving the portfolio slightly up pre-pandemic (2000-2019) and costing more than 2% this summer.
vol_and_positioning: Investors hedge against higher policy rates using derivatives that pay off if rates rise more than priced, because bonds no longer hedge equities.
Lopsided demand for rate protection pushes market-implied rates above the expected path.
The October tech sell-off triggered a rotation into other equities and bonds. Stocks and bonds moved in opposite directions again, and the Fed premium fell from well over 100bp to about 30bp.
Large equity gains may have amplified the demand for protection. Handelsbanken says its data has too few such episodes to establish this with confidence.
geopolitical: Middle East conflict and energy prices: bad news pushes energy prices up and sustains the supply-shock regime
De-escalation or a deal in the Middle East could shrink the rate premium quickly, while escalation or a longer road to a deal would keep it elevated

tension_points.bull_case: Market pricing of about three Fed hikes is a premium for rate protection rather than an expectation. Forecasters expect one hike, and market rates could fall by more than policy expectations if Middle East tensions ease and bonds hedge equities again.
tension_points.bear_case: Escalation or a longer road to a deal keeps the supply-shock regime in place. Stocks and bonds keep moving together, expected policy rates could rise, and a wider premium could amplify the rise in market-implied rates.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Stocks and bonds returning to opposite moves, as after the October tech sell-off when the Fed premium fell to about 30bp, would shrink the premium. A rising stock-bond correlation, as seen in November, would widen it.

theme_stances.key_argument: Market pricing overstates the expected policy path because investors pay for protection against higher rates, so forecasts deserve more weight.
theme_stances.evidence: Market pricing currently overstates the expected policy path.

theme_stances.key_argument: Supply shocks make stocks and bonds fall together, so bonds no longer hedge equities and 60/40 portfolios carry more risk.
theme_stances.evidence: Supply shocks turn this relationship around.
